subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage: Eshaan, when your Nani taught Class Four in Nagpur, the children called me Shalini Madam. There was a boy, Manoj, who always laughed first at my jokes. One winter he changed. He slumped over his desk, yawned through dictation and snapped at his bench-mate over a pencil. I nearly sent him out for not paying attention. Instead, at break, I asked him quietly how he was sleeping. He told me his family had moved into one room beside the railway line, and the night trains shook the walls. I spoke to his mother, who found him a corner away from the tracks, and I stopped marking him down for slow mornings. By spring his laugh was back.

qa.q: What shook the walls at Manoj's new home?
qa.a: The night trains.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when Manoj snapped over the pencil?
qa.a: She felt irritated enough to nearly send him out, but also puzzled, because he had always been so cheerful.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Shalini handled Manoj, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing to ask him quietly about sleep at break instead of punishing him; it uncovered the noisy trains, which a punishment would have hidden.

qa.q: What might that winter have been like for Manoj?
qa.a: He was probably worn out and cross from broken sleep, and being punished for it would have felt unfair.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a usually cheerful child turn slumped and irritable, and asking gently about sleep instead of punishing.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage: The inspection team was due at eleven, and Raghav Sir wanted Class Three quiet and tidy. Tenzin, usually the first to wave good morning, sat slumped with his cheek on his fist, notebook unopened. When a classmate bumped his elbow, he growled, "Leave me alone!" Raghav felt the clock pressing on him; a punishment would be quicker. He crouched beside Tenzin anyway. "You seem very tired today. When did you get to bed?" Tenzin rubbed his eyes. "After tuition I had two worksheets. And my cousins were staying, so the TV was loud." Raghav let him start with the easier page and wrote in his diary for his parents: "Tenzin seems very tired. Can we talk about homework and bedtime?"

qa.q: When was the inspection team due?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: Why was Raghav tempted to punish Tenzin?
qa.a: He felt pressured and anxious about the inspection, and a punishment seemed quicker than finding out what was wrong.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped, and what could come next?
qa.a: He asked kindly about bedtime and eased Tenzin in with an easier page; next, talking with the parents about homework and noise could fix the cause.

qa.q: How might the morning feel for Tenzin if he had been punished?
qa.a: He would likely feel misunderstood and more upset, and the real problem of late nights would stay hidden.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher under time pressure noticing a normally cheerful child's slump and temper and asking about bedtime, homework and noise.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage: Ishita was usually the first hand up in Pradeep Sir's Class 5 in Indore, full of jokes. This week she sat slumped, snapped at her bench partner over an eraser, and was still staring at a blank page ten minutes after everyone had started. Pradeep felt the old urge to say, "Pay attention or stand outside." Instead, at break, he crouched by her desk. "You seem really tired. How's bedtime been?" Ishita rubbed her eyes. "They're building a flyover next to our building. The drilling goes on all night." Pradeep nodded. He gave her a shorter worksheet for the day, moved her to the quiet seat by the window, and wrote a note home asking whether she could nap in the afternoons until the drilling moved on.

qa.q: What is being built next to Ishita's building?
qa.a: A flyover.

qa.q: What was Pradeep tempted to do, and what made him hold back?
qa.a: He felt a flash of irritation and an urge to send her outside, but he held back because he was puzzled and concerned that his cheerful student had changed so much.

qa.q: Which of Pradeep's steps would help most while the drilling goes on?
qa.a: The note home asking about afternoon naps, because it tackles the missing sleep itself, while the shorter worksheet and quiet seat ease the day.

qa.q: What is school like for Ishita this week?
qa.a: She is exhausted and short-tempered, struggling to start work and snapping at her bench partner, far from her usual cheerful self.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a normally cheerful child slumped and irritable and asking gently about bedtime and noise instead of punishing her.

"Kiran, stay back a minute. You're not in trouble."
"Okay, Ma'am."
"You yawned all through science. And you told Riya to shut up. That's not like you."
"Sorry. I'm just tired."
"What time did you sleep last night?"
"Twelve. After abacus class and Hindi tuition I still had my project."
"Is it like that every night?"
"Most nights. I keep saying I'll be fast, but I'm slow when I'm sleepy."
"That makes sense. Tired brains are slow brains. Can I talk to your mother about the homework load?"
"Will she be angry?"
"I'll tell her you were honest. And today, no extra practice sheet. Go home and rest."
Afreen Ma'am wrote a reminder on her hand before the next bell rang.

qa.q: What time did Kiran sleep last night?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: How can you tell Afreen feels concerned rather than annoyed?
qa.a: She tells Kiran there is no trouble and calls the rude words "not like you", which shows care and worry rather than anger.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that was more useful than a punishment?
qa.a: She asked gently about bedtime and homework, found the real cause, and planned to talk with Kiran's mother about the load.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel walking home without the extra practice sheet?
qa.a: Kiran is likely relieved and understood, because the tiredness was noticed instead of punished.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a child's yawning and short temper and asking gently about bedtime and homework load rather than punishing.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage: Last term I nearly punished Swati for sleeping in my maths class. She was the girl who hummed while doing sums, always first to laugh at my terrible jokes. For a week she yawned, put her head down, and once kicked her chair when I called on her. I had the detention slip half written. Then I remembered my own bad months as a student, and after class I asked her, softly, how she was sleeping. Her family had moved in with relatives, she said, and she slept in the hall, where the TV ran till one. I phoned her mother that evening, and they moved her mattress into the small storeroom. Two weeks later Swati was humming again. I, Ganga, still keep that unfinished detention slip in my drawer.

qa.q: Till what time did the TV run in the hall?
qa.a: Till one.

qa.q: Why does Ganga keep the unfinished detention slip?
qa.a: Ganga seems relieved and a little ashamed at how close that punishment came, and keeps the slip as a reminder to ask first.

qa.q: What made asking gently work better than detention?
qa.a: It uncovered the late TV in the hall, and a call to her mother led to a quieter place for Swati to sleep.

qa.q: What was that week like for Swati?
qa.a: She was exhausted and irritable, too tired to hum or laugh, and possibly worried about being in trouble.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a cheerful child slumped and irritable, and asking about noise at home instead of punishing her for inattention.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4A
Madhav is usually the one cracking jokes at the start of the day. This week he has been slumped on his desk, yawning, snapping at his partner and taking ages to open his notebook. My first thought on Tuesday was to send him to the headmistress for not working. I held back and asked him quietly at lunch how he was sleeping. He said his baby sister cries at night, the family shares one room, and he has been doing homework late. I have cut his homework this week and will speak to his mother on Friday about a quieter bedtime corner.
Harish

qa.q: Why has Madhav been sleeping badly?
qa.a: His baby sister cries at night, the family shares one room, and he has been doing homework late.

qa.q: What was Harish's first impulse on Tuesday, and what feeling was behind it?
qa.a: Harish felt frustrated and was tempted to send Madhav to the headmistress for not working.

qa.q: Why was the quiet question at lunch the better choice?
qa.a: It uncovered the real cause, lost sleep, so Harish could cut homework and plan with the family instead of punishing.

qa.q: What might it be like for Madhav to be asked kindly instead of punished?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and understood, since he was too tired to work, not lazy.

grounding: A teacher notices a cheerful child slumped and irritable and asks gently about sleep instead of punishing.
